title: Rio Blanco County Wells: Depth, Yield and Cost
meta_description: Rio Blanco County wells have an 80-foot median depth. Compare local yields, water levels, permit history and finished-well costs of $10,000-$18,000.
h1: What to Expect from a Well in Rio Blanco County
intro_html:
A shallow county median does not guarantee a shallow well on your lot. Rio Blanco County’s reported wells have a median depth of 80 feet, but the middle half spans 34-230 feet. That spread matters when you price land around Meeker or Rangely.

Colorado DWR records contain 3,450 permits in the county, with 1,690 recorded as constructed. These records cover more than household water supplies, so use the county figures as a starting point, then compare nearby wells with similar uses and ground conditions.

sections.heading: An 80-Foot Median, but a Wide Drilling Range
sections.html:
Of the 1,413 wells reporting depth, 54% are under 100 feet. Another 27% fall between 100-300 feet, while 8% are 300-600 feet and 11% are 600 feet or deeper. The 90th-percentile depth is 697 feet. A bid based only on the 80-foot median can miss substantial deeper-ground exposure.

The ground is mixed sedimentary and alluvial. Most permits carry an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer label; 102 name Alluvial and 11 name Uinta. Those broad labels do not establish what lies beneath a particular parcel. Ask the driller to compare nearby completion logs and explain how the 34-230-foot middle range affects the estimate and extra-depth charges.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Favor Household Supply, Not Guarantees
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 12.5 gpm, with the middle half at 7.0-15.0 gpm. That is encouraging for household supply, but only 290 wells report yield. The sample also includes nonhousehold uses: domestic/household permits account for 37% of county records, stock for 18%, irrigation for 13% and monitoring for 17%.

Among reported yields, 2% are under 1 gpm and 10% are in the 1-5 gpm band. A low-producing well may need storage and careful demand planning. A recorded pump yield is not a guarantee of sustained delivery today. Before buying, request a current pumping and recovery test rather than relying on the permit’s original figure.

sections.heading: Water Often Stands Shallow, Without a Clear Decline
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth to standing water when the well is not pumping, not the depth of the drilled hole. Across 217 reported measurements, the median is 20 feet below ground, and the middle half is 6-58 feet. A deeper well can still have water standing relatively close to the surface.

Decade medians move from 40 feet in the 1960s to 10 in the 1970s, 28 in the 1990s, 13 in the 2000s, 24 in the 2010s and 18 in the 2020s. This series does not show a steady decline. These are different groups of measurements, not repeated readings from a single monitoring network, so they cannot establish a parcel-level trend.

sections.heading: What Rio Blanco’s Permit History Tells You
sections.html:
Permit issuance rose from 203 in the 1970s to 323 in the 1990s, 624 in the 2000s and 810 in the 2010s. The 2020s account for 438 permits, with the newest dated 2025. That is an incomplete decade, and issuance does not necessarily mean a well was completed.

Prominent driller-field entries include Water Pump Supply & Service (Day, Travis), with 237 records, and Water Pump Supply And Service (Day, Winfred C.), with 145. The largest listed entry, Authorized (Pe, Pg), has 290 records but is not a clear business name. Treat these as historical record labels, not confirmation of current availability or licensing.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Hole in Meeker or Rangely
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $50-$75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the county’s 80-foot median, that puts the drilled hole around $4,000-$6,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $10,000-$18,000.

Those figures are a planning allowance, not a parcel quote. With the middle half of reported depths spanning 34-230 feet, depth alone can change the job substantially. Get a written scope identifying casing, grout, development, testing and the route to the house. Confirm what is included in the per-foot price and what happens if the initial target does not produce usable water.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Keep the Site Buildable
sections.html:
The surrounding mapped inventory includes 224 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 12 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These map counts do not establish contamination in an individual well. Review each relevant site’s status and location, then use a certified laboratory and local health guidance to choose testing for the property.

Inspect the wellhead, casing condition and surface drainage as well as the water itself. A producing well can still have water-quality problems. For a new build, resolve well and septic placement, approved separation requirements, drilling access and the house footprint together. Do not leave septic feasibility until after the well and driveway locations are fixed.

sections.heading: Before Closing on a Rio Blanco County Lot
sections.html:
Start with neighboring completion records around the actual parcel, not just the county median or a listing’s claim that water is available. Meeker and Rangely have their own local pages for a closer comparison. Garfield County and Moffat County provide regional context, but nearby wells in comparable ground are more useful than a distant county average.

Verify the DWR permit, permitted uses and well location. Do not assume household authorization includes irrigation or stock watering. On an existing well, obtain pumping, recovery and water-quality results. On vacant land, make the purchase decision with a drilling scope, a contingency for inadequate production and a workable septic and access plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Rio Blanco County, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported wells have an 80-foot median depth, with the middle half between 34 and 230 feet. Although 54% are under 100 feet, 11% are 600 feet or deeper. The figures come from 1,413 depth reports across different well uses. Nearby completion logs are a better guide to your lot than the county median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Rio Blanco County?
faq.a: The local model uses $50-$75 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $4,000-$6,000, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $10,000-$18,000. Ask for a parcel-specific quote that identifies casing, grout, testing, access requirements and charges for drilling deeper than expected.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Rio Blanco County?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 12.5 gpm, and the middle half is 7.0-15.0 gpm. Only 290 wells report yield, so this is not a complete picture of county supplies. Reported yields under 1 gpm account for 2%. Have an existing well tested for sustained pumping and recovery before judging whether it meets your household needs.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Rio Blanco County?
faq.a: The permit statistics cannot establish drinking-water safety. The mapped area includes 224 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 12 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but proximity does not prove a well is affected. Review relevant site records and obtain property-specific laboratory testing, along with an inspection of the wellhead and casing.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Rio Blanco County?
faq.a: The supplied measurements do not show a steady countywide decline. Median static water depth was 24 feet in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s, with earlier decades also fluctuating. These summaries combine different wells and measurement conditions. For a purchase, look for historical readings from the same well and obtain a current static-level and pumping assessment.
